span-16b1.name: Berlin Endgame
span-16b1.annotation: The most analyzed endgame in the world

scot-7a.name: Classical Scotch
scot-7a.annotation: Central space and damaged black structure

sic-9a1.name: Najdorf
sic-9a1.annotation: The most played in the world

fr-5a.annotation: Attacks the base of the chain

al-1.name: Alekhine's Defense
al-1.annotation: Provokes White's advance to attack it

al-3.annotation: The knight retreats with a future plan

al-6c.name: Four Pawns Attack
al-6c.annotation: The most aggressive, massive pawn chain

qg-2.name: Queen's Gambit
qg-2.annotation: Offers the pawn for central control

qg-3a.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
qg-3a.annotation: Accepts the gambit; White recovers the pawn

qg-4a.annotation: Development and threat to recover the pawn

qg-3b.name: Queen's Gambit Declined
qg-3b.annotation: Declines maintaining the center with e6

qg-3c.name: Slav Defense
qg-3c.annotation: Reinforces d5 without blocking the queen's bishop

qg-5c.annotation: Develops the knight and defends d5

qg-7c1.name: Accepted Slav
qg-7c1.annotation: Accepts the gambit with c6 support

qg-8c2.annotation: Opens the center to exploit the structure

qg-7c3.name: Classical Variation
qg-7c3.annotation: Develops the bishop before closing with e6, the key Slav idea

qg-8c3.annotation: Consolidates the center without closing the bishop yet

qg-10c3.annotation: Prepares the bishop exchange on d3

qg-12c3.annotation: Recaptures activating the queen in the center

qg-4ce.name: Exchange Variation
qg-4ce.annotation: Simplifies the center with cxd5, seeking equality with a symmetrical structure

qg-5ce.annotation: Recaptures with the pawn maintaining symmetry

qg-6ce.annotation: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, key idea of the Exchange

qg-7ce.annotation: Develops the knight to c6 with central pressure

qg-8ce.annotation: Consolidates with e3 before completing development

qg-10ce.annotation: Completes development and coordinates the pieces

qg-11ce.annotation: Develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain

qg-12ce.annotation: Increases pressure on d5 with the knight

lon-2.name: London System
lon-2.annotation: Solid setup without committing to c4

lon-4.annotation: Active bishop before closing the chain

lon-6.annotation: Consolidates the center without sharp exchanges

ki-5a.annotation: The powerful Indian bishop on the long diagonal

ki-7a.annotation: Prepares e5 to attack the center

ki-11a1.annotation: The typical Indian break, generates dynamic play

ki-10a2.name: Main Sämisch
ki-10a2.annotation: Targets the dark squares on the kingside

nim-3b.name: Nimzo-Indian / Queen's Indian
nim-3b.annotation: Prepares Bb4 pinning the c3 knight

nim-6b1.name: Classical Nimzo
nim-6b1.annotation: Avoids doubling pawns, pressure on c4

nim-6b2.name: Rubinstein Nimzo
nim-6b2.annotation: Solid and classical, consolidates the center

dutch-1.name: Dutch Defense
dutch-1.annotation: Black weakens e5 to attack the kingside

dutch-5a.name: Leningrad Variation
dutch-5a.annotation: Aggressive fianchetto with bishop on g7

dutch-11b1.name: Complete Stonewall
dutch-11b1.annotation: Solid and closed position for Black

mod-1.name: Modern Defense
mod-1.annotation: Hypermodern: Black cedes the center to attack it with pieces

mod-3.annotation: Fianchetto: the bishop will dominate the long diagonal

mod-6a.name: Austrian Attack
mod-6a.annotation: Most aggressive: f4 prepares f5 and a central push

nw-1.name: Nimzowitsch Defense
nw-1.annotation: Hypermodern opening: 1...Nc6 lets White occupy the center to attack it later

nw-2.annotation: White occupies the center with d4

nw-4a.annotation: 3.e5 advances gaining space, ceding control of d5

nw-4b.annotation: 3.exd5 opens the game, Black's queen comes to d5

nw-4c.annotation: Normal development, preparing to recapture the pawn

nw-5a.annotation: Bishop actively developed outside the pawn chain

nw-6b.annotation: White develops the knight, attacking the queen on d5

nw-6c.annotation: Knight centralizes on d4, dominating the center

nw-7a.name: Advance Variation
nw-7a.annotation: Black consolidates with e6, limiting White's bishop behind the chain

nw-7b.name: Exchange Variation
nw-7b.annotation: Pin with Bg4, pressuring White's knight on f3

nw-7c.name: Kennedy Variation
nw-7c.annotation: Knight development, preparing castling and dynamic counterplay

nf3.name: Zukertort Opening
nf3.annotation: Hypermodern opening: White develops the knight without committing the center, with the option of 2.b3 (Zukertort proper) or many transpositions

zuk-2.name: Queenside Fianchetto
zuk-2.annotation: With 2.b3, White prepares Bb2 and adopts the Zukertort proper: center control from a distance, without directly occupying it

zuk-4a.annotation: The bishop on b2 pressures the long diagonal toward e5 and d4. White completes development before deciding whether to advance e3 or g3

zuk-8a.name: Classical Variation
zuk-8a.annotation: After 1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Nf6 3.Bb2 e6 4.e3 Be7 5.d4, White establishes a solid structure. Plan: Nd2-e5 followed by central pressure

zuk-8b.name: Double Fianchetto (Nimzo-Larsen)
zuk-8b.annotation: With 3...g6 and 4.g3, both sides fianchetto their kingside bishops. Closed strategic positions where control of the long diagonals is the key

zuk-8c.name: Reversed Pirc
zuk-8c.annotation: After 2.b3 c5 3.Bb2 Nc6 4.e3 e5 5.d4, Black aggressively seizes the center. White responds with d4, initiating tactical central tension

zuk-1b.name: Ross Gambit
zuk-1b.annotation: With 1...e5, Black offers the king pawn in a questionable gambit. Bold but theoretically inferior: White simply captures with a material advantage

zuk-4c.name: Ross Gambit Accepted
zuk-4c.annotation: After 1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 d6 3.Nf3, White consolidates the material advantage. Black seeks compensation through rapid development, but the position is objectively favorable for White

marshall-1.name: Marshall Defense
marshall-1.annotation: With 2...Nf6, Black defends d5 with a piece instead of a pawn. This unorthodox response to the Queen's Gambit trades central control for piece activity and quick development.

marshall-2.annotation: The capture 3.cxd5 is White's most direct response. White gains central space and forces Black to decide how to recapture.

marshall-3a.name: Main Line
marshall-3a.annotation: With 3...Nxd5, Black recaptures with the knight, maintaining a flexible structure but allowing White to gain a tempo with 4.e4.

marshall-4a.annotation: The advance 4.e4 attacks the knight on d5 and establishes a dominant pawn center. White achieves a significant space advantage.

marshall-5a.annotation: The knight must retreat. 4...Nf6 is the most natural square, returning to f6 to continue development.

marshall-6a.name: Classical Variation
marshall-6a.annotation: 5.Nc3 develops naturally and prepares e5 to drive the Black knight again. White holds a clear central space advantage with good piece coordination.

marshall-3b.name: Tan Gambit
marshall-3b.annotation: With 3...c6, Black sacrifices a pawn for quick development and central pressure. This is the most aggressive and ambitious response to 3.cxd5.

marshall-4b.annotation: White accepts the sacrifice by capturing on c6. Black will recapture with the knight, gaining rapid development in return.

marshall-5b.annotation: With 4...Nxc6, Black recovers the material and activates the queen's knight, targeting e5 for central tension.

marshall-6b.annotation: 5.Nf3 is White's most solid development. White prepares to complete development and maintain the material advantage.

marshall-7b.annotation: 5...e5 is the central thrust that justifies Black's pawn sacrifice. Black seeks equality through piece activity.

marshall-8b.annotation: 6.e3 restrains Black's central advance and prepares to recapture on d4 with a positional advantage.

marshall-9b.name: Tan Gambit — Main Line
marshall-9b.annotation: After 6...exd4 7.exd4, White retains a small extra pawn but Black has active compensation. The position is roughly balanced with White holding a slight edge.

marshall-3c.name: Grünfeld Attempt
marshall-3c.annotation: With 3...g6, Black tries to transpose into Grünfeld territory, seeking a more familiar position. However, White can prevent the transposition precisely.

marshall-4c.name: Qa4+ Refutation
marshall-4c.annotation: 4.Qa4+ is the precise response that frustrates the transposition attempt. Black cannot recover the d5 pawn and is left with a weakened kingside structure.

evans-1.name: Evans Gambit
evans-1.annotation: With 4.b4, White offers a pawn to open lines and seize a devastating initiative. One of the most aggressive openings of the 19th century, revived by Kasparov in the 1990s.

evans-2a.name: Evans Gambit Accepted
evans-2a.annotation: Black accepts the pawn with 4...Bxb4, entering sharp tactical waters. White will regain material with a development and space advantage.

evans-2b.name: Evans Gambit Declined
evans-2b.annotation: With 4...Bb6, Black refuses the gambit and maintains structure, avoiding tactical complications at the cost of some initiative.

evans-3a.annotation: 5.c3 prepares d4. White builds a powerful pawn center and threatens to drive the bishop away with tempo.

evans-4a.annotation: The main retreat. 5...Ba5 keeps the bishop active and waits for White to commit the center.

evans-4b.name: McDonnell Defense
evans-4b.annotation: 5...Bc5 is the McDonnell Defense. Black returns the bishop to c5, but White responds with 6.d4 gaining tempo.

evans-5a.annotation: The central strike 6.d4 is the most aggressive continuation. White opens the position and activates all the pieces.

evans-5b.annotation: 6.O-O prepares the Lasker Defense. White castles before d4, giving Black an opportunity to consolidate.

evans-6a.annotation: 6...exd4 accepts complications. Black captures in the center but White obtains enormous positional compensation.

evans-6b.annotation: 6...d6 is Bronstein's solid response. Black reinforces e5 and waits for the tactical battle to develop.

evans-7a.annotation: 7.O-O develops with a threat. White castles and threatens to regain the pawn with attacking initiative.

evans-7b.name: Tartakower Attack
evans-7b.annotation: 7.Qb3 is the Tartakower Attack. The queen simultaneously threatens f7 and b4, maintaining maximum pressure on Black.

evans-7c.annotation: 7.d4 in the Lasker line activates the center. White seeks to exploit Black's delay before consolidation.

evans-8a.name: Mieses Defense
evans-8a.annotation: 7...Nge7 is the Mieses Defense, a modern and solid approach. The knight supports d5 and avoids direct kingside tactics.

evans-8b.annotation: 7...dxc3 is the Compromised Defense. Black keeps the extra material but the position comes under enormous tactical pressure.

evans-8c.name: Lasker Defense
evans-8c.annotation: 7...Bb6 is the famous Lasker Defense. The bishop retreats to balance the position and Black seeks simplification.

evans-8d.annotation: The normal McDonnell Defense position after 8...d6. Black has a solid position but White retains the initiative.

evans-9b.annotation: 8.Qb3 attacks f7 and a4 simultaneously. White regains material while maintaining the attack in the Compromised Defense.

evans-10b.name: Compromised Defense
evans-10b.annotation: 8...Qf6 defends f7 in the Compromised Defense. Black has two extra pawns but the position is extremely difficult to defend.

evans-3b.annotation: 5.a4 threatens to trap the bishop on b6. White switches plans to the queenside to exploit the bishop's position.

evans-4c.annotation: 5...a6 is the Showalter Variation response, stopping a5. Black halts White's advance and prepares counterplay.

evans-5d.name: Showalter Variation
evans-5d.annotation: 6.Nc3 completes the Showalter Variation. White develops with queenside pressure, and Black must play accurately to maintain balance.

philidor-3.name: Philidor Defense
philidor-3.annotation: With 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6, Black reinforces the e5-pawn in a solid but passive manner. The central idea is to maintain the pawn chain and develop with ...Nd7 or ...Nf6, accepting a slightly cramped position in exchange for great structural solidity.

philidor-5a.name: Exchange Variation
philidor-5a.annotation: 3...exd4 immediately releases the central tension. White recaptures with 4.Nxd4 and gains a small space advantage while Black seeks equality through quick development.

philidor-9a.name: King's Bishop Line
philidor-9a.annotation: 5...Be7 is Black's most solid response. It prepares short castling and maintains a compact structure before committing to a development plan.

philidor-17a1.name: Exchange Variation Main Line
philidor-17a1.annotation: After 6.Bf4 O-O 7.Qd2 Nc6 8.O-O-O Nxd4 9.Qxd4 Be6, White has castled queenside with a slight space edge. Black has active counterplay with ...a6 and ...Nd7 to challenge the queenside.

philidor-10a2.name: Antoshin Variation
philidor-10a2.annotation: 6.Be2 prepares short castling and avoids complications with Bf4. Named after Soviet grandmaster Vladimir Antoshin, this variation aims for solid positions where White gradually exploits a small spatial advantage.

philidor-14a2.name: Antoshin Variation — f4 Line
philidor-14a2.annotation: After 6.Be2 O-O 7.O-O Re8 8.f4, White adopts an aggressive kingside pawn advance. Black counterattacks in the center with ...d5 or on the queenside.

philidor-5b.name: Hanham Variation
philidor-5b.annotation: 3...Nd7 is the hallmark move of the Hanham Variation. The knight defends the e5-pawn without blocking the c8-bishop, keeping a compact and flexible position.

philidor-12b.name: Hanham Variation — Ng5 Attack
philidor-12b.annotation: After 4.Bc4 c6 5.O-O Be7 6.dxe5 dxe5 7.Ng5, White directly attacks f7. This tactical position demands precision from Black; the main continuation is 7...Bxg5, returning material to stabilize.

philidor-5c.name: Nimzowitsch Variation
philidor-5c.annotation: 3...Nf6, named for Aaron Nimzowitsch, immediately attacks the e4-pawn. It is the second most popular response in the Philidor Defense, leading to more active positions for Black.

philidor-7c1.name: Lion Variation
philidor-7c1.annotation: 4.Nc3 Nbd7 forms the Lion Variation, where Black builds a very solid position with two knights guarding the center. White must play carefully to maintain the space advantage.

philidor-11c1.name: Lion Variation — Castled
philidor-11c1.annotation: After 4.Nc3 Nbd7 5.Bc4 Be7 6.O-O O-O, both sides have completed basic development. Black has a solid though somewhat passive position; the typical plan involves ...c6 and ...Re8 to press the center.

pon-1.name: Ponziani Opening
pon-1.annotation: With 3.c3, White prepares the central advance 4.d4. One of the oldest recorded openings, favored by Ponziani in the 18th century.

pon-2a.name: Jaenisch Counterattack
pon-2a.annotation: 3...Nf6 targets e4, exploiting the fact that c3 prevents White from playing Nc3.

pon-5a.annotation: 5.d5 drives the c6-knight away and gains space.

pon-6a.annotation: 5...Ne7 is the solid retreat for the c6-knight.

pon-7a.name: Jaenisch Counterattack
pon-7a.annotation: 6.Nxe5 captures with initiative. White holds material and spatial advantages.

pon-3b.annotation: 4.Qa4 pins the c6-knight against Black's king.

pon-4ba.annotation: 4...f6 (Steinitz Variation) defends e5 with a pawn, though weakening the a2-g8 diagonal.

pon-6ba.annotation: 5...Nge7 develops the kingside knight preparing Qxd5.

pon-8ba.name: Steinitz Variation
pon-8ba.annotation: 6...Qxd5 centralizes the queen. Black has an active position but still faces pressure on c6.

pon-4bb.annotation: 4...Nf6 (Leonhardt Variation) develops the knight and attacks e4.

pon-5bb.annotation: 5.Nxe5 captures e5, exploiting the pin on the c6-knight by Qa4.

pon-6bb.annotation: 5...Bd6 attacks the e5-knight and develops a bishop.

pon-8bb.name: Leonhardt Variation
pon-8bb.annotation: 6...bxc6 opens the b-file. Black obtains the bishop pair as compensation for doubled pawns.

pon-2c.name: Ponziani Countergambit
pon-2c.annotation: 3...f5 offers a pawn to seize immediate initiative and unbalance the position.

pon-3c.annotation: 4.d4 fights for the center rather than accepting the gambit.

pon-4c.annotation: 4...fxe4 accepts the gambit, creating immediate tactical tension.

pon-5c.name: Ponziani Countergambit
pon-5c.annotation: 5.Nxe5 leads to the sharpest play. The position is tactically complex and double-edged.

falk-1.name: Falkbeer Countergambit
falk-1.annotation: Black's aggressive response to the King's Gambit. With 2...d5, Black creates immediate central tension and tactical compensation.

falk-3.annotation: The classic King's Gambit pawn sacrifice.

falk-4.annotation: The Falkbeer Countergambit: Black sacrifices d5 to seize the initiative.

falk-5.annotation: Accepting the countergambit. The alternative 3.fxe5?? loses to 3...Qh4+.

falk-6a.name: Charousek Gambit
falk-6a.annotation: Modern main line. White stabilizes with d3.

falk-13a.name: Charousek Main Line
falk-13a.annotation: Standard position with bishop on f5. White has space advantage; Black has dynamic compensation.

falk-5b.annotation: Nimzowitsch-Marshall Defense: Black seeks piece activity via 3...c6.

falk-9b.annotation: Bishop to g4, pressuring the knight.

falk-11b.name: Nimzowitsch-Marshall Variation
falk-11b.annotation: Black pushes e5, seeking centralization. Dynamic play for both sides.

falk-6c.name: Anderssen Attack
falk-6c.annotation: Active alternative: Bishop to b5+ instead of d3.

falk-11c.name: Anderssen Attack Main Line
falk-11c.annotation: Black captures the pawn. Complex position with resources for both sides.
